evidence.claim: Route 49 has two designated scenic sections: one north from Route 184 toward Voluntown, and another from the Voluntown boat launch to Sterling.
evidence.quote: Route 49 is designated as a scenic road from Route 184 (milepost 2.09) in North Stonington to milepost 12.95 (south of Route 165) in Voluntown and from the Voluntown boat launch (milepost 13.84) to the northern terminus in Sterling.

evidence.claim: This road once carried the number 95. Assigned that number in 1932, it extended east to the Rhode Island line in 1950.
evidence.quote: In the 1932 state highway renumbering, State Highway 216 was renumbered to Route 95. In 1950, Route 95 was extended east along modern Route 14A up to the Rhode Island state line.

evidence.claim: Interstate 95’s designation in 1958 created a numbering conflict, so the older road became Route 49.
evidence.quote: In 1958, Interstate 95 was formally designated in Connecticut, and Route 95 was in need of a new designation due to the numbering conflict. The new designation chosen was Route 49.

evidence.claim: The creation of Route 14A in 1963 moved Route 49’s northern end to its present junction.
evidence.quote: In 1963, as a result of the Route Reclassification Act, Route 14A was created and the north end of Route 49 was relocated to its current terminus.

evidence.claim: A corridor management effort began in 2003 with speed, stone walls and scenery among its concerns. That October, the state refused North Stonington’s request to lower the speed limit from 45 mph to 35 and 30 mph.
evidence.quote: In early 2003, work on Route 49 and Route 14A Corridor Management Plan was started, funded by the FHWA and ConnDOT. The concerns are speed along Route 49, stone walls, and the surrounding scenery.

evidence.claim: A corridor management effort began in 2003 with speed, stone walls and scenery among its concerns. That October, the state refused North Stonington’s request to lower the speed limit from 45 mph to 35 and 30 mph.
evidence.quote: In October 2003, the state turned down a North Stonington request to lower the speed limit from 45 mph (72 km/h) to 35 and 30 mph (48 km/h).

evidence.claim: From Sterling Hill on Route 14A, take Route 49 south along Ekonk Hill Road through the forest and across the Pachaug River.
evidence.quote: Route 49 continues as Ekonk Hill Road, crossing the Pachaug River and running through the Pachaug State Forest, before reaching its end at Route 14A in the Sterling Hill Historic District

evidence.claim: In Voluntown center, the road briefly shares Routes 165 and 138, then continues south as Westerly Road.
evidence.quote: Route 49 then becomes Westerly Road, while still on a northward track. Route 49 briefly overlaps with Route 165 and Route 138 within the town center.

evidence.claim: In North Stonington, it becomes Pendleton Hill Road and reaches Route 184.
evidence.quote: It proceeds north into the town of North Stonington as Pendleton Hill Road, intersecting with Interstate 95 and Route 184.

evidence.claim: Sterling Hill’s church began as a town hall. The town voted to build it in 1797 and made it available to a Baptist congregation in 1812.
evidence.quote: The town voted in 1797 to build a town hall, which in 1812 was made available to a Baptist congregation for religious use.

evidence.claim: It is now the Sterling Hill Baptist Church, with Greek Revival styling added in 1859.
evidence.quote: This is the present Sterling Hill Baptist Church, which was given Greek Revival styling in 1859.

evidence.claim: The village stands where Plainfield Pike meets Sterling Hill Road and Route 49.
evidence.quote: The historic district is centered around the junctions of Plainfield Pike with Sterling Hill Road (which leads north) and Connecticut Route 49 (which leads south).

evidence.claim: French troops camped overnight here in 1781 and again in 1782.
evidence.quote: The French camped overnight in Sterling Hill, both in 1781 and in 1782.

evidence.claim: Industrial development and the railroad bypassed the village during the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: The village center was entirely bypassed by industrial development in the 19th century, and by the railroad

evidence.claim: The historic district includes houses in Federal, Greek Revival and Italianate styles, clustered around those road junctions.
evidence.quote: the district includes 14 older and newer houses that include Greek Revival, Italianate, and Federal architecture.

evidence.claim: Pachaug grew substantially during the Great Depression. Established in 1928, the forest acquired most of its land through later Depression-era purchases.
evidence.quote: The forest was founded in 1928, but most of the land came from purchases made later during the Great Depression.

evidence.claim: Its parcels now cover more than 27,000 acres across six towns, making it Connecticut’s largest state forest.
evidence.quote: Pachaug State Forest is the largest forest in the Connecticut state forest system, encompassing over 27,000 acres

evidence.claim: Its parcels now cover more than 27,000 acres across six towns, making it Connecticut’s largest state forest.
evidence.quote: parcels of the forest lie in the towns of Voluntown, Griswold, Plainfield, Sterling, North Stonington, and Preston.

evidence.claim: The Pachaug River runs through its center and gives it its name.
evidence.quote: It is named after the Pachaug River, which runs through the center of the forest.

evidence.claim: Great Meadow’s Atlantic white cedar swamp earned National Natural Landmark status in 1973.
evidence.quote: The Pachaug-Great Meadow Swamp portion of the park was declared a National Natural Landmark in May 1973 due to its Atlantic white cedar swamp.

evidence.claim: Elsewhere, the Rhododendron Sanctuary Trail includes a wooden boardwalk section.
evidence.quote: Rhododendron Sanctuary Trail (which includes a planked wooden boardwalk section)

evidence.claim: Rhododendrons bloom in June and July along that sanctuary trail, in the Herman Haupt Chapman Management Area of the forest.
evidence.quote: Rhododendron Sanctuary Trail (which includes a planked wooden boardwalk section) in the Pachaug State Forest's Herman Haupt Chapman Management Area is spectacularly scenic when the Rhododendron are in bloom (June and July).

evidence.claim: Voluntown’s name refers to colonial volunteers in King Philip’s War in 1675.
evidence.quote: The town was named for the colonial volunteers in the 1675 King Philip's War

evidence.claim: Lieutenant Thomas Leffingwell helped secure legislative approval for the town and surveyed its original layout.
evidence.quote: One of the founders of Voluntown was Lieutenant Thomas Leffingwell, who secured the town's approval in the colonial legislature and surveyed its original layout.

evidence.claim: The modern road changes names here: Route 49 is Ekonk Hill Road north of the center and Westerly Road to the south.
evidence.quote: Route 49 then becomes Westerly Road, while still on a northward track.

evidence.claim: The modern road changes names here: Route 49 is Ekonk Hill Road north of the center and Westerly Road to the south.
evidence.quote: North of the overlap, Route 49 continues as Ekonk Hill Road

evidence.claim: Between them, it shares Routes 165 and 138 through town.
evidence.quote: Route 49 briefly overlaps with Route 165 and Route 138 within the town center.

evidence.claim: On Ekonk Hill Road, the Wylie School preserves another part of town history. Used until 1939, it is Voluntown’s only surviving district school building, with two matching entrances leading toward a single schoolroom.
evidence.quote: this school was used by the town until 1939, and is its only surviving district school building.

evidence.claim: On Ekonk Hill Road, the Wylie School preserves another part of town history. Used until 1939, it is Voluntown’s only surviving district school building, with two matching entrances leading toward a single schoolroom.
evidence.quote: The Wylie School is located in a rural setting, at the northern corner of Ekonk Hill Road (Connecticut Route 49) and Sandhill Road.

evidence.claim: On Ekonk Hill Road, the Wylie School preserves another part of town history. Used until 1939, it is Voluntown’s only surviving district school building, with two matching entrances leading toward a single schoolroom.
evidence.quote: Its main facade has two matching entrances, framed by simple molding and topped by a cornice.  The interior has two vestibules with closets between them, leading into a single large schoolroom
